figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of drug screening methods.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 2. Application of ML and DL in drug screening. ML and DL are novel methods that combine AI technology to perform HTS drug screening. The process begins by 
establishing a screening model with a training dataset for algorithm development and a validation set for testing, where ML relies on experts for feature extraction, 
while DL automates information organization, reducing subjective bias. In drug screening, known compounds from databases (natural products, clinical drugs, 
chemical drugs, etc.) are scored and the top hits are selected for validation through experiments. The representative compounds screened through ML and DL, and 
their corresponding activities are displayed.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 3. Basic processes and applications of in vitro drug screening. (A) Molecular networking. MS data is denoised, merged, and analyzed for similarity to generate 
molecular network. Integrating network with activity data, top hits are selected, purified and finally validated. (B) Genetic engineering. Genetic engineering creates 
desired disease models for HTS, with positive hits validated through biochemical assays to confirm efficacy and mechanism of action. (C) Active protein. Target 
proteins are identified, purified, and used in HTS to find interacting compounds. The efficacy of potential compounds is validated through further assays.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 4. Drug screening through cellular spheroids. Cellular spheroids are powerful tools in drug screening and can be generated through different methods, which can 
be divided into scaffold-free (A–F) and scaffold-based (G) formation. Following preparation using these methods, cellular spheroids can be used for experiments such 
as HTS, cell viability assessments, cell imaging assays for drug screening purposes (H).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 5. Application of organoid in drug screening. Organoids are typically derived from iPSCs or tissue-derived cells (TDCs). Cancer stem cells (CSCs), in particular, 
have extensive applications in this field (A). Single cells are isolated and seeded onto specific biologically derived matrices, such as extracellular matrix (ECM) 
substrates, for the aggregation to embryoid bodies (B). Through adjusting the physical, chemical, and biological conditions of the culture system, generation of 
organoids is facilitated. The harvested organoids can be applied into physiological parameter investigation, histologic assessment, and multi-omics analysis for drug 
screening (C). Several examples of organoids and their potential active compounds identified through organoids (D).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 6. Application of organ-on-a-chip in drug screening. The organ-on-a-chip consists of living cells and microfluidic channels that mimic the structure and function 
of tissues, allowing the study of organ behavior, disease progression, and drug response in a controlled, dynamic environment. Drug activity was investigated through 
imaging techniques and various biochemical assays (A). The application of organ-on-a-chip in drug screening is shown (B).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 7
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 7. The application of C. elegans in drug screening. C. elegans is a powerful model organism widely used in drug screening studies. Through behavioral assays, it 
can be used to screen drugs for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases (A). C. elegans can be utilized to screen anthelmintics, with survival assays evaluating 
drug efficacy due to its classification as parasitic worms like Ascaris and tapeworms (B). Its short lifespan makes it an ideal model for screening anti-aging drugs 
through lifespan assays (C). It can be infected by multiple human pathogens, making it valuable in antimicrobial experiments (D). With genes homologous to humans 
and ease of genetic manipulation, C. elegans is commonly used in studying gene function and drug mechanisms through experiments like RNAi treatment (E).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 8
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 8. The utilization of Drosophila in drug screening. Drosophila is a powerful model organism for various experiments. For example, target models can be created 
through gene editing, in vivo imaging can be performed using techniques like immunofluorescence, and survival states can be observed through behavioral assays. 
Both larvae (A, B) and adults (C ~ F) can be used in drug screening.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 9
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 9. The application of zebrafish in drug screening. Zebrafish are characterized by their small size and short breeding cycles, making them an ideal vertebrate 
model for HTS (A). Advanced gene editing techniques enable the construction of specific disease models, where certain target proteins can be tagged with fluorescent 
markers, facilitating detection (B). The transparency of larval zebrafish allows for clear observation of internal structures following staining procedures (C). Owing to 
the high genetic homology between zebrafish and humans, zebrafish can accept human tumor transplants to establish robust tumour-bearing models (D). Behavioural 
observation through recording zebrafish activity trajectories provides valuable insights into their physiological and survival status (E).
